The ambassador of the Romans, however, was not willing at first, and said:
"The Arab prisoners who are with us are all soldiers whom we captured in battle,
while the Christian prisoners who are with you are mostly peasants whom you captured from villages, old men and old women, and little boys and girls;
and how shall we give soul for soul?" And when they had disputed over this for days,
at last the ambassador agreed to exchange one for one.
And because the number of Arab prisoners reached four thousand three hundred and sixty-two souls,
and the Christian prisoners were fewer than this number,
King al-Wathiq sent and gathered from all his territories whatever male and female slaves he could find, purchasing them from their masters;
and when even so the number was not filled,
he brought out from his own palace Roman maidservants whom he had chosen for himself, and sent them with his ambassadors.
And the Arabs and the Romans gathered at the river of Seleucia, which is in the territory of Tarsus,
and the release took place.
And it is said that al-Wathiq commanded his ambassadors:
"Every Arab whom you ransom from chains,
first ask him:
'Is the Word of God created or not?' And him who answers, 'Not created',
ransom;
but him who [says], 'Created',
leave in the hands of the Romans."
Now al-Wathiq died of the affliction of dropsy (accumulation of water).
For the physicians were treating him with an oven that was heated.
And when he found some relief in this,
he commanded, and the bath-attendants heated it more than the rule;
and he went down and lingered in it,
and from there they brought him out dead.
Up to this point the kings of the Arabs had been concerned with victories and triumphs,
but from here on they were given over to great neglect
and occupied themselves with drunkenness.
This al-Wathiq was entirely wanton and dissipated,
so that for the price of a certain singing maidservant, one hundred thousand gold dinars and the governorship of Egypt were demanded by her master.
And had he not been rebuked by his treasurers,
without doubt
he would have given it.
In the end, however, they acquired her for him for ten thousand [pieces of] gold.
After al-Wathiq [reigned al-Mutawakkil] fourteen years and nine months.
And he began to reign in the year 231 [of the Arabs].
